artists.biography: The Cinematic Orchestra is a British jazz and electronic outfit, created in 1999 by Jason Swinscoe. The band is signed to independent record label Ninja Tune. In addition to Swinscoe, the band includes former DJ Food member PC (Patrick Carpenter) on turntables, Luke Flowers (drums), Tom Chant (Saxophone), Nick Ramm (piano), Stuart McCallum (guitar) and Phil France (double bass). Former members include Jamie Coleman (trumpet), T. Daniel Howard (drums), Federico Ughi (drums), Alex James (piano), and Clean Sadness (synthesizer, programming). The most recent addition to the band is Mancunian guitarist Stuart McCallum. Swinscoe and Carpenter (PC) have also recorded together under the band name Neptune.

perplexity.description:
To Believe represents The Cinematic Orchestra's fourth studio album and their first full-length release in twelve years, arriving in March 2019 on Ninja Tune. The record maintains the group's signature blend of orchestral arrangements and jazz-inflected downtempo production while embracing an ambitious collaborative approach. Thematically centered on belief amid contemporary uncertainty, the album navigates the darker musical landscape of the late 2010s without abandoning the emotional gravitas and sophisticated instrumentation that define the project.

The album's structure emphasizes vocal contributions from carefully selected guest artists, including Moses Sumney on the understated opener, Roots Manuva on the more hopeful "A Caged Bird / Imitations of Life," and Heidi Vogel among others, balanced by only two purely instrumental tracks. Each collaboration demonstrates restraint and precision rather than excess, with layered production featuring orchestral strings, jazz harmonies, and electronic textures working in concert to create atmospheric depth. The result showcases Jason Swinscoe's continued ability to synthesize complex arrangements into emotionally resonant compositions.

Critical reception positioned To Believe as a triumphant return that achieved comparable standing to its predecessor Ma Fleur, with reviewers highlighting the album's emotional sophistication and the quality of its guest performances. The record charted modestly across international markets while reinforcing The Cinematic Orchestra's status as one of Britain's most respected acts in the nu jazz and electronic music spheres.
